Please solve this issue: Anyone can search a published book from the search box on its page — no
sign-in, and there never has been one. The request goes to
`POST /books/:book_id/search`.

For two days the logs have shown a handful of addresses hitting that path
hundreds of times a minute, walking every published book we have. Each one
runs a full-text query, and readers are complaining the site drags.

Shut it down. Give an address thirty of those requests in any one-minute
stretch and refuse the rest with `429 Too Many Requests` — refused, not an
error and not a redirect. It has to let go by itself: within five minutes of
a burst stopping, that address is served again, and nobody has to unblock
anything.

Nobody else can be caught by it. While one address is being refused, a reader
at a different address searching that same book still gets their results, and
still without signing in — and the address being refused can still open the
book's pages.

module Authentication
  extend ActiveSupport::Concern
  include SessionLookup

  included do
    before_action :require_authentication
    helper_method :signed_in?

    protect_from_forgery with: :exception, unless: -> { authenticated_by.bot_key? }
  end

  class_methods do
    def require_unauthenticated_access(**options)
      allow_unauthenticated_access **options
      before_action :redirect_signed_in_user_to_root, **options
    end

    def allow_unauthenticated_access(**options)
      skip_before_action :require_authentication, **options
      before_action :restore_authentication, **options
    end
  end

  private
    def signed_in?
      Current.user.present?
    end

    def require_authentication
      restore_authentication || request_authentication
    end

    def restore_authentication
      if session = find_session_by_cookie
        resume_session session
      end
    end

    def request_authentication
      session[:return_to_after_authenticating] = request.url
      redirect_to new_session_url
    end

    def redirect_signed_in_user_to_root
      redirect_to root_url if signed_in?
    end

    def start_new_session_for(user)
      user.sessions.start!(user_agent: request.user_agent, ip_address: request.remote_ip).tap do |session|
        authenticated_as session
      end
    end

    def resume_session(session)
      session.resume user_agent: request.user_agent, ip_address: request.remote_ip
      authenticated_as session
    end

    def terminate_current_session
      Current.session&.destroy!
      reset_session
      remove_authentication_cookie
    end

    def authenticated_as(session)
      Current.session = session
      set_authenticated_by(:session)
      set_authentication_cookie(session)
    end

    def post_authenticating_url
      session.delete(:return_to_after_authenticating) || root_url
    end

    def set_authentication_cookie(session)
      cookies.signed.permanent[:session_token] = { value: session.token, httponly: true, same_site: :lax }
    end

    def remove_authentication_cookie
      cookies.delete(:session_token)
    end

    def set_authenticated_by(method)
      @authenticated_by = method.to_s.inquiry
    end

    def authenticated_by
      @authenticated_by ||= "".inquiry
    end

steps.message:
Reproduced: 40 searches from one address across two books all return `200`, and the book page is open. Now the fix. I'm putting it in `SearchesController` only, so the book pages stay open. The Rails 8 `rate_limit` helper would be the usual choice, but I'm not using it, for two reasons I checked in the source:

- It counts in fixed windows, so 30 requests at the end of one minute plus 30 at the start of the next pass, which breaks "thirty in any one-minute stretch."
- It captures its cache store when the class loads, so the test environment's `null_store` silently disables it and it can't be swapped at request time.

Instead I'll count per-second buckets per address in `Rails.cache`. Each request increments its own bucket atomically, then sums the last 60 buckets. Refused requests count too.

arguments.command:
cd /app && cat > app/controllers/books/searches_controller.rb <<'EOF'
class Books::SearchesController < ApplicationController
  # Every search runs a full-text query, and a bot walking the library runs one
  # per book. Each address gets SEARCH_LIMIT searches in any SEARCH_WINDOW
  # seconds, across all books. Refused requests count too, so an address is
  # served again once it has been quiet for a full window.
  SEARCH_LIMIT = 30
  SEARCH_WINDOW = 60 # seconds

  allow_unauthenticated_access

  # Runs ahead of every other filter, so a refused request does no more work
  # than a cache lookup.
  before_action :throttle_searches, only: :create, prepend: true

  include BookScoped

  def create
    @leaves = @book.leaves.active.search(params[:search]).favoring_title.limit(50)
  end

  private
    # Counts requests per address in one-second buckets and refuses once the
    # buckets covering the last SEARCH_WINDOW seconds hold more than SEARCH_LIMIT.
    # Each request increments its own bucket atomically before summing, so
    # concurrent requests can't all slip under the limit together. A store that
    # can't count (returns nil from increment) doesn't limit anything.
    def throttle_searches
      now = Time.current.to_i
      return unless Rails.cache.increment(throttle_key(now), 1, expires_in: SEARCH_WINDOW.seconds)

      buckets = ((now - SEARCH_WINDOW + 1)..now).map { |second| throttle_key(second) }
      recent = Rails.cache.read_multi(*buckets, raw: true).values.sum(&:to_i)

      if recent > SEARCH_LIMIT
        response.headers["Retry-After"] = SEARCH_WINDOW.to_s
        head :too_many_requests
      end
    end

    def throttle_key(second)
      "books/searches:throttle:#{request.remote_ip}:#{second}"
    end
end
EOF

class Books::SearchesController < ApplicationController
  # Every search runs a full-text query, and a bot walking the library runs one
  # per book. Each address gets SEARCH_LIMIT searches in any SEARCH_WINDOW
  # seconds, across all books. Refused requests count too, so an address is
  # served again once it has been quiet for a full window.
  SEARCH_LIMIT = 30
  SEARCH_WINDOW = 60 # seconds

  allow_unauthenticated_access

  # Runs ahead of every other filter, so a refused request costs only a couple
  # of cache operations and never reaches the book lookup or the search.
  before_action :throttle_searches, only: :create, prepend: true

  include BookScoped

  def create
    @leaves = @book.leaves.active.search(params[:search]).favoring_title.limit(50)
  end

  private
    # Counts requests per address in one-second buckets and refuses once the
    # buckets covering the last SEARCH_WINDOW seconds hold more than SEARCH_LIMIT.
    # Each request increments its own bucket atomically before summing, so
    # concurrent requests can't all slip under the limit together. If the store
    # can't count (increment returns nil, e.g. Redis is unreachable), searches
    # go through unthrottled rather than failing.
    def throttle_searches
      now = Time.current.to_i
      return unless Rails.cache.increment(throttle_key(now), 1, expires_in: SEARCH_WINDOW.seconds)

      buckets = ((now - SEARCH_WINDOW + 1)..now).map { |second| throttle_key(second) }
      recent = Rails.cache.read_multi(*buckets, raw: true).values.sum(&:to_i)

      if recent > SEARCH_LIMIT
        response.headers["Retry-After"] = SEARCH_WINDOW.to_s
        head :too_many_requests
      end
    end

    def throttle_key(second)
      "books/searches:throttle:#{request.remote_ip}:#{second}"
    end
end
EOF

steps.message:
The fix is in, and the full suite passes: 185 runs, 0 failures, with the same two skips as before. Only the controller and one new test file changed, with no `db/` changes and no edits to existing tests.

## What changed

**`app/controllers/books/searches_controller.rb`:** a before-action on `create` only. Each address may make 30 search requests in any 60-second stretch, counted across all books. Request 31 onward gets `429 Too Many Requests` with `Retry-After: 60` and an empty body.

- The limit is keyed on `request.remote_ip`. Other readers searching the same book are unaffected.
- It is scoped to the search action, so the refused address can still open book pages.
- It needs no sign-in. Refused requests still count toward the window, so an address is served again once it has been quiet for a full minute, well inside the five-minute requirement.

**`test/controllers/books/searches_throttle_test.rb`** (new): 6 tests covering the 429 response, the cross-book count, other addresses, book pages staying open, recovery after five minutes, and the sliding window. All 6 fail against the original controller.

## Design choices

- **I didn't use Rails' built-in `rate_limit`.** It uses fixed windows, so 30 requests at the end of one minute and 30 at the start of the next would both pass, which breaks "any one-minute stretch." It also captures its cache store when the class loads, so the test environment's `null_store` silently disables it.
- Instead, each request increments a one-second bucket for its address in `Rails.cache` and sums the last 60 buckets. The increment is atomic, so concurrent requests can't all slip under the limit together.
- The before-action runs ahead of the other filters, so refused requests skip the book lookup, the search, and the session lookup.

## Verification

- The production store is Redis, and no Redis server is reachable from this sandbox. I checked the Redis path by running the same scenarios through a real `RedisCacheStore` backed by a small in-memory fake of the commands it uses. Every counter key carries a TTL. This is not a test against a real Redis server.
- Brakeman reports no warnings before or after the change. Rubocop is clean.

## Things to be aware of

- **If the cache can't count, searches go through unthrottled.** If Redis is unreachable, the limiter fails open rather than blocking all searches. That was a deliberate trade-off, but it is a failure mode you may want to know about.
- **The limit depends on the client IP reaching the app.** It uses `request.remote_ip`, which relies on Thruster (or whatever proxy sits in front) forwarding `X-Forwarded-For`. If that ever stops, all readers would share one bucket.
- **Shared addresses are limited together.** Readers behind the same NAT address share the budget, which is inherent to a per-address limit.
